body: When would something like this happen?
That will make the __ functions slower, as mark asks when would that happen? sounds like an edge case.

This happened to me when I pulled data out of the db and passed some field values to __(). The first argument happened to be null (the db allows null values as defaults).

So it's not a matter of throwing notices and fixing my code; this only came to light because of a null value in my db. I know about the array signature, and that's what I switched to, but a null first argument still shouldn't negate the rest of the replacements. If the value is null, I'd expect the respective %s to be replaced with an empty string.

From a API standpoint, I'd rather be forced to use the array() signature and be sure it's safe than having to test and "fix" my first argument before passing it to __().
Having a ~~non-empty~~ empty value for a replacement would in most cases result in an incomplete/non-meaningful translated string anyway.

> From a API standpoint, I'd rather be forced to use the array() signature and be sure it's safe than having to test and "fix" my first argument before passing it to __().

What's wrong with 

```
__('whatever %s %s', (string) $var ...)
```

if $var is potentially null (I would say that's not really normal/expected) ensuring it's a string prevents the problem.

> From a API standpoint, I'd rather be forced to use the array() signature

I agree - but it's a choice that currently exists.
Since the cast or the array syntax is an easy solution for this edge case here we can probably close as works-for-me.

My issue is that it fails silently. Unlike a php function that throws a notice or warning when an argument is the wrong type.  

I guess it feels like "unexpected" behaviour to me because I'm accustomed to sprintf() replacing with an empty string when you pass in a null value.

Anyway, if this is "expected" behaviour I think the docs should be updated to mention that the only safe way to use it when passing in multiple arguments is via cast or array syntax.

It is worth noting that this issue effects all of the `__*` functions inthe same way. While I agree that using an array is better, we cannot remove the var args call style right now.

One option would be to add another argument and test if both are null. This doesn't fully solve the issue though. It merely reduces the chances of this occuring.

If null is the only problem here, it would be possible to change the function declaration to maybe
  function __($singular, $args = false) {
and later test for the default value of args accordingly to 
  if ($args === false) {
this, however will render it impossible to pass false as the second argument instead of null...

On the other hand, I would be willing to bet that the suggested fix of
  if ($args === null && func_num_args() < 3) {
will not slow down the function noticably, because php like c and many other languages does evaluate the conditions von left to right, which means that the second operand will not even be evaluated if the first is not true in this case.
- Try that for yourself with in arbitrary function call instead of func_num_args() as the second operand!
  This means that it will - if at all - take one assembler instruction more, if args !== null, which is the default case that matters.

Having said this - please test yourself that the second operand is really not even evaluated if the first is false anyway - the suggested fix is the absolute right way to go!

Props for CostaC on that one!
@hmic I would just put up a gist with the code, and results.
